extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners responsible for designing, implementing, and evaluating PR programs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for planning, implementing, measuring, and reporting public relations program effectiveness, including research steps, levels of evaluation, preparation and implementation criteria, and measurement methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be numeric as well as rhetorical
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations practitioners must learn basic skills in math and statistics to generate and present data to inform, support, test, manage, and evaluate their programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many PR practitioners come from arts/humanities and deal in rhetoric; management is numbers-oriented. There is no way to sugarcoat this: practitioners must be number-literate to communicate with management and to perform credible evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formative and summative research (evaluation research types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research conducted before and during implementation to inform planning and program adjustment is called formative research; research conducted after the program to assess progress and document impact is called summative research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both types fall under 'evaluation research' or 'measurement'; use formative research to shape programs and summative to assess outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation research definition (systematic assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation research is 'the systematic application of social research procedures for assessing the conceptualization, design, implementation, and utility of social intervention programs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes evaluating preparation, implementation, and impact of PR programs; evaluation should learn what happened and why, not merely justify prior decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program conceptualization and design criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions to assess program conceptualization and design: What is the extent and distribution of the target problem/population? Is the program designed in conformity with intended goals with a coherent rationale and maximized chances of delivery? What are projected or existing costs and their relation to benefits and effectiveness?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These questions guide evaluation of whether the program's design matches the problem and objectives and whether costs are justified by expected benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring and accountability of program implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the program is reaching the specified target population/area and whether intervention efforts are being conducted as specified in the program design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This stage focuses on implementation fidelity and reach; it helps identify breakdowns between planned and actual activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of program utility: impact and efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the program is effective in achieving intended goals; whether results can be explained by alternative processes; whether the program has unintended effects; what are the costs to deliver services and benefits; and whether the program is an efficient use of resources compared with alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation here examines causal attribution, unintended consequences, cost-benefit relationships, and comparative efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid symbolic or pseudoresearch
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation research should be done honestly and objectively to provide data for decision making with an open mind; symbolic evaluation (pseudoresearch) is conducted to provide supportive data for decisions already made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common motivations for pseudoresearch: organizational politics (to gain power or justify decisions), service promotion (slanted research to impress clients), and personal satisfaction (ego-driven faddish research). Such efforts are self-defeating in the long run.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1: Establish agreement on uses and purposes of the evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Commit to paper the problem, concern, or question that motivates the research effort and detail how research findings will be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without such agreement, research often produces volumes of unused/useless data; written statements are doubly important when hiring outside specialists to avoid buying 'canned' services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2: Secure organizational commitment to evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Make research basic to the program; evaluation cannot be tacked on as an afterthought and must have sufficient resources to be central to problem definition, planning, implementation, and evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed research throughout the program lifecycle so evaluation is feasible and meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 3: Develop consensus on using evaluation research within the department
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure practitioners, including those who value creativity and 'intangibles', accept research as necessary to build the strategic foundation, while recognizing it will not replace creativity and experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gain buy-in from all staff to avoid resistance and to integrate evaluation with practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 4: Write program objectives in observable and measurable terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Program objectives must specify measurable outcomes; without measurable outcomes specified, evaluation research cannot be designed to evaluate program impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an objective outcome cannot be measured, it is not useful; write specific objectives for each target public to enable evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 5: Select the most appropriate criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose measurement criteria that directly reflect the objectives (e.g., if objective is increasing awareness of support for charities, use knowledge measures rather than column inches or favorable mentions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify what changes in knowledge, opinions, attitudes, and behaviors are specified before gathering evidence; avoid substituting implementation measures for impact measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 6: Determine the best way to gather evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Select methods (surveys, organizational records, field experiments, case studies) based on the motivating question/purposes, outcome criteria in the objectives, and the cost of approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no single right way; method choice depends on question, specified outcomes, and cost/complexity of the program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 7: Keep complete program records
rubrics_metrics.description: Document program strategies and materials as real-world expressions of practitioners' working theories of cause and effect to help identify what worked and what did not work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete documentation reduces selection perception and personal bias when reconstructing contributors to success or failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 8: Use evaluation findings to manage the program
rubrics_metrics.description: Use each cycle of evaluation to make adjustments so problem statements, situation analyses, goals, objectives, and strategies reflect what was learned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should inform continuation, fine-tuning, or discarding of actions and communication strategies based on evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 9: Report evaluation results to management
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a procedure for regularly reporting to line and staff managers to document results and adjustments based on evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular reporting shows that PR is managed to contribute to organizational goals or 'bottom lines.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 10: Add to professional knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Share evaluation findings with colleagues to contribute cross-situational understanding even though most program evaluation tends to be specific to an organization and time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disseminating relevant findings distinguishes professional practice from technical craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levels/stages of program evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation can be conceptualized as stages: preparation/inputs, implementation/outputs, and impact/outcomes/effects (also referenced as inputs, outputs, impact, and effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best-practice approaches recommend addressing criteria at all levels; common error is substituting measures from one phase (implementation counts) for those of another (impact).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation evaluation: Information Base
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the adequacy of background information used for planning: Were key publics missed? What assumptions were in error? Were required facts unavailable? Were key actors identified?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic assessment and recording of missing information during a program provide intelligence for planning the next program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation evaluation: Program Content
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess organization and appropriateness of program and message content (pretesting brochures, websites, speeches, scripts) to determine if content is appropriate to target publics and objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review accuracy, timeliness, appropriateness, adverse reactions, support from action components, staff and budget adequacy; use content analysis of materials and media coverage as part of this evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation evaluation: Presentation Quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess technical and production values of messages and other program elements (style, format, presentation merit) using both subjective expert judgement and objective readability/listenability measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readability tools (Gunning Fog Index) and listenability measures (Irving Fang's ELF) give quantitative indicators of reading/listening difficulty, but do not account for jargon, content, organization, or audience context; use them as guides alongside qualitative assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation evaluation: Distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Document the number of messages/materials produced and distributed (letters, news releases, feature stories, PSAs, website updates, speeches, broadcast appearances, exhibits), and record such activities to show implementation as planned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribution records help trace unsatisfactory results to breakdowns in distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation evaluation: Placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the number and quality of messages placed in media (earned media usage) because placement determines whether target publics had opportunity for exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clipping/monitoring services and maintain up-to-date press contact lists; poor placement (e.g., sending materials to people no longer at outlets) can nullify otherwise effective materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject AVEs (Advertising Value Equivalents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising value equivalents (AVEs) are inappropriate measures of PR effectiveness because editorial coverage is not equivalent to paid advertising; AVE calculations are flawed and misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons AVEs fail: editorial can be irrelevant/negative/competitor-inclusive/poorly positioned/poorly presented; AVE measures cost not value; multipliers and 'third-party endorsement' weightings are unsupported by research. Prefer content analysis and impact measures instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media content analysis variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Content analysis typically examines place or position, prominence, share of voice, issues or topics, messages (favorable/unfavorable), and visuals (photos, footage, logos), using both quantitative and qualitative coding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place/position: e.g., page 1 or lead TV item has greater impact; Prominence: mention in headline/first paragraph; Share of voice: amount of space/time relative to competitors; combine quantitative coding (tone counts) with qualitative discourse/text analysis for deep insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential audience vs effective audience (audience reach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate delivered audience (all potential readers/viewers/listeners) from effective audience (those who are in target publics). Audience reach measures the effective audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use audited circulation and audience data (e.g., ABC, Nielsen, Arbitron) and demographic/psychographic segmentation; beware that social media 'counting metrics' (users, followers, page views) may be 'digital trivia' and not evidence of effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attentive audience (measuring attention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how many of the delivered audience actually paid attention (readership, listenership, viewership). Use recognition/recall techniques such as Daniel Starch's 'noted', 'associated', and 'read most' levels (aided recall).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readership studies and aided recall can indicate depth of attention (e.g., 'read most' = read at least 50% of copy); online attention metrics and studies also used but must be interpreted carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience measurement methods (diary, meter, people meter, telephone interview)
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary methods for measuring broadcast audiences: diary (self-recorded logs), meter (electronic set tuning logs), people meter (individual buttons for household members), and telephone interviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each method has biases/limitations: diary participants may differ from nonparticipants; meters may not detect who/how many are watching; people meters burden participants and may miss some sets; telephone interviews are another option. Choose methods with awareness of their limitations.
